blocks.text: It is proved that איה aja is a species of hawk, which the ancients call the aesalon, the Germans Smirle, and we esmerillon [merlin].

After the treatise On the Eagle we tried to explain three names of birds, namely פרס peres, עזניה oznija, and דאה daa, or ראה raa, which are found nowhere outside the catalogue of unclean birds. Since in interpreting these the ancient and modern interpreters disagree greatly, their true meaning could be extracted from no other source than the origin of the words alone. Now four follow, namely איה aja, דיה daja, עורב oreb, and בת־יענה bath-jaana; since these are found elsewhere, more light will shine on their explanation. Yet there is much doubt about the first. The Greeks explain it sometimes as vulture, sometimes as kite. [col. 193] The former is followed by Jerome, Munster, Pagninus, Castalio, and the English and Italian versions; the latter by the Arabic translator in Job, Schindler, and the Genevans. Jonathan renders it דייתא אוכמתא, black vulture; the Jerusalem Targum, אבו ibbu, which I think is the same. Onkelos has טרפיתא, bird of prey, a generic name, because he did not know the species. The Arabs in Moses have الصدا [al-ṣadā] owl. Kimchi has יגא״וא, magpie. Junius and Buxtorf, magpie or crow. Arias, variegated bird. Pomarius, vulture or hawk. Aben Ezra, island bird, as if the name were formed from אי, that is, from island. Other Hebrews, such as R. Levi, Mordecai, and Aquinas, more prudent than the rest, say only that it is שם עוף, the name of a bird.
